headline: Expands the ban on U.S. courts and agencies recognizing trademarks tied to businesses the Cuban government confiscated.
what_it_does: Before this law, U.S. courts could not enforce or approve trademarks confiscated by the Cuban government, but only when a Cuban national was claiming them. This law extends the ban to federal executive agencies and applies it no matter who claims the mark, if the mark was used with a confiscated business or asset. The ban does not apply if the original owner, or whoever took over their rights, clearly agrees. It also applies only if the party claiming the mark knew or should have known, when it got the rights, that the mark matched or closely resembled one tied to a confiscated business or asset.

who_it_affects.group: Original owners of Cuban businesses whose trademarks were confiscated, and their successors
who_it_affects.how: Others generally cannot enforce or register their former marks in the U.S. without their express consent.

who_it_affects.group: Companies and people (Cuban or not) seeking to use or protect trademarks tied to confiscated Cuban businesses
who_it_affects.how: U.S. courts and federal agencies may refuse to enforce or approve those marks if the claimant knew or should have known of the link to a confiscated business.

who_it_affects.group: Federal executive agencies that handle trademarks
who_it_affects.how: They are now also barred from recognizing or enforcing these confiscated trademarks.

when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted December 1, 2024; the summary does not give a separate effective date.
